newsitem.title: USA: Chile hits Helms-Burton before talking to Congress.
newsitem.headline: Chile hits Helms-Burton before talking to Congress.

text.p: President Eduardo Frei of Chile on Thursday criticized as counterproductive a U.S. law aimed at promoting democracy in Communist-ruled Cuba.
Before going to Congress to urge speedier negotiation of free trade with Chile, Frei said the Helms-Burton law had failed in its goal of encouraging democracy and human rights in Cuba.

"It has been counter-productive," he told a National Press Club news conference, speaking through an interpreter. "I believe the Helms-Burton law is a law of intervention in the free rights of a nation."

The law enacted last March by a Republican-led Congress has angered Europeans, Canadians, Mexicans and other U.S. allies who accuse Washington of trying to force their hand on sanctions aimed at ousting Cuban President Fidel Castro, a thorn in the side of every U.S. president since he seized power in 1959.

In his speech to a joint meeting of Congress, Frei did not mention Helms-Burton but warned against impediments to free trade and called for higher-level negotiations with the United States on a free trade deal. "Our trade negotiations with the United States are of great interest to us and we believe they should advance to higher levels," he said.

Chile was invited in December, 1994, to join the United States, Mexico and Canada in the North American Free Trade Agreement. But it wants Congress to give the administration "fast-track" authority to cut a deal that would be voted on without any amendments pushed by special interest groups.

"Before this Congress, let me reaffirm our interest in those negotiations," Frei said. "We consider total trade liberalization between Chile and the United States a natural step, as well as an encouraging signal in the task of achieving free trade in Americas."

The White House faces big problems in getting Congress to pass the negotiating authority essential to cutting trade deals with Chile and others. Such "fast-track" authority ensures that a trade pact would get a straight yes-or-no vote.
After meeting Frei at the White House on Wednesday, President Bill Clinton called on lawmakers to grant him the authority, put on hold during last year's election campaign.

House of Representatives Minority leader Richard Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat, wrote in a letter to his Democratic colleagues on Wednesday that it would be "a fundamental mistake to simply extend the current NAFTA. It simply isn't working."

Frei said he hoped it would not be as hard to get free trade talks going as had often been the case with peace talks in this century. "Delays today could mean the weakening of many democracies, the rebirth of closed markets, the consolidation of hunger and migrations," he said.

In a Spanish-language interview on the CBS-Telenoticias network moments before addressing the House and Senate, Frei said he did not expect his criticism of Helms-Burton to hurt prospects for passage of "fast-track" legislation.
